utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: As I indicated last week, we would have a hearing this morning on the Prosecution's motion for judicial notice of adjudicated facts; and to facilitate the hearing, we had distributed three areas which we would like the parties to concentrate on. Let me just inquire whether you received them. This was done on Friday. Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, my memo has two questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Two.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes, not three. But I'm happy to try to handle the third question, if you put it to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, you should be able to.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, I'll do my best.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. And I'd like to focus the hearing along those lines, so I don't want the parties simply to get up and start a recitation of the -- of what was their motion and the response given by the Defence. And so the first question that I identified was, "How does one distinguish between a factual finding and a finding of an essentially legal nature?" Because we don't take judicial notice of the latter, of legal conclusions, and we give an example, "Proposed Fact 166, which says, "Civilians in ABiH-held areas of Sarajevo were directly or indiscriminately attacked from SRK-controlled territory between September 1992 and August 1994." The question there being whether that's a finding of fact or a finding of an essentially legal conclusion with particular reference to the words "directly or indiscriminately attacked." The second question was -- and this relates to the same issue, but we thought we would highlight it because it occurs so frequently. "Does the term 'civilian' denote a legal conclusion as to the status of a victim or, for example, of a building or an object?" And an example of that would be proposed fact 178: "The SRK attacked civilians, men and women, children and the elderly in particular, while engaged in typical civilian activities, or were expected to be found in a similar pattern of conduct throughout the city of Sarajevo between September 1992 and August 1994." Now, the third area is perhaps the most -- the most difficult, and I don't know if this is the one which you don't have.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry to interrupt, but just to be clear, actually, all three areas are on the memo. The first two questions that you identified were merged into one question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: -- and so it is covered, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. This is how we put the third question: "In cases where the proposed facts," and I'm sorry, we should have passed this on to the interpreters; my apologies, "in cases where the proposed facts do not go toward the acts, conduct or mental state of the Accused, should these facts nonetheless be excluded following" Karemera's Appeals Chamber decision on the basis that admitting them would "not advance Rule 94(B)'s objective of achieving expediency without compromising the rights of the accused, particularly the right to cross-examine? "For example, are the rights of the Accused safeguarded for those facts which - albeit from the pre-Indictment period - will be relied upon by the Prosecution as evidence going to prove that the Accused knew, should have known, or was put on notice that crimes had been or were about to be committed for the purposes of establishing criminal responsibility." I imagine you're familiar with the Karemera Appeals Chamber decision, and these essentially are facts which do not go to the acts and conduct of the accused and, therefore, might be admitted on that basis. But when you take into account the wider interests of justice and the -- when you seek to balance the objectives of expediency with the rights of the accused, particularly his right to examine, you may very well conclude that the rights of the accused are compromised. And we identified a number of factors -- a number of facts, rather, proposed facts, following into this category, taken from the Galic judgement. So let us hear first from Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And I understand I have 25 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. I see now what was distributed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes. And I understand I have about 25 minutes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will go straight away to address the two or three questions put by the Trial Chamber. But first I would like to take just two minutes to set the stage of the issue, because I do think that this becomes relevant to answering the second of the two questions that have been put by the Trial Chamber. As Your Honours are aware, the Prosecution filed its motion on December 18th of 2006, and the Defence responded over a month later, on January 19, 2007. The Defence, and this is what I think is critical, made a single objection to the proposed facts which are in dispute, which are facts 54 to 181. It's a single objection which is expressed in exactly two sentences. And the objection they make is that those facts are not relevant to this case. That is the only objection that they made. Now, of course, the Trial Chamber has an independent obligation, as does the Prosecution, to protect the rights of the accused. However, in our view, that has to be - that has to be - in the context of the chosen defence of the accused. If the rights of the accused mean anything, they have to mean the right to choose one's defence, what the defence will be. And here we would suggest that what the Defence has done is indicated, through its response, that its defence is something along the lines of, Whatever happened in -- from 1992 to 1994, that is not relevant to this case which focuses on 1994 to 1995. And that might be for a number of reasons. That could be because when the accused took over the command of the SRK, things changed. He changed things so that they were different. So what happened in 1994 to 1995 was different; or it may be that whatever happened in 1994 to 1995, he is not responsible for it. There are a number of reasons why -- a number of perfectly coherent reasons why 1994 is -- could be different from the point of view of the Defence than 1992 to 1994. So the point is the Defence says -- what they say is, Don't admit those facts because they are not relevant; they have no bearing on this issue. You cannot argue from those facts anything that occurred from 1994 to 1995, because for some reason what happened in that second phase was different. Now, I would ask Your Honours to hold that in your minds because, as I said, that will become an important point in response to the second question. Now, of course, we say that what happened in 1992 to 1994 is relevant, and I don't take the questions from the Trial Chamber as disputing that or putting that into question, let's say. We say it's relevant, 1992 to 1994, because it was the establishment, the creation, the putting into place, of an ongoing crime which the accused then inherited in 1994, in August of 1994, inherited and continued. Not only that, but the Prosecution will offer evidence to show that the accused - and this is evidence which is separate, of course, from the adjudicated facts - that the accused held a responsible position -- responsible positions from 1992 to 1994 within the SRK, which meant that he was both a part of putting this criminal plan, criminal scheme, into place, and he was put on notice of it. Mr. President, I think you summarised or you captured what the Prosecution's argument may be once the adjudicated facts are put together with other facts that the Prosecution will prove about that period, 1992 to 1994, and that is that, number 1, the accused was instrumental and a part of putting together -- putting that criminal scheme into place, and he was certainly aware of it; and number 2, and this is very critical, in August of 1994, when he became the commander of the SRK, he continued that scheme and did nothing to stop it. And it's very important for the Prosecution to be able to prove that this scheme was in place, and by "the scheme," of course, I mean the campaign of shelling and sniping against civilians; that that scheme was in place already by August of 1994, and the accused was well aware of it and he did nothing to stop it but, in fact, perpetuated it. Now, if I could go to Your Honours' questions. The first question with respect to distinguishing between a factual finding and a legal finding. If Your Honours don't mind, I'm going to combine the two examples that Your Honours provided, the indiscriminate attack example and the civilian -- the identification of a civilian example, into one -- essentially one issue. The language that the Trial Chamber has identified, whether it's a factual finding or an essentially legal finding, of course, comes from the Krajisnik decision of 24 March 2006. And the important word, of course, is "essentially." In our view, none of the facts that we have proposed, including the facts that have been identified by the Trial Chamber in its questions, are of an essentially legal nature. Now, Karemera, the Karemera Appeals Chamber decision, is actually highly instructive on this issue, if not determinative. The first section of Karemera -- of course, we've been focusing on the second section which deals with 94(B). The first section of the opinion deals with 94(A), which is a different section but has commonalities with 94(B). 94(A) deals with -- what's the word? It's facts that are known -- common facts which are in within common knowledge as opposed to adjudicated facts, and there are some differences between those two sections which are identified by Karemera. However, one thing that is the same, 94(A) and 94(B), is that it's only facts and not legal conclusions which may be admitted. Whether they're commonly known or previously adjudicated, it can only be facts. And I would point Your Honours to the discussion in 94 -- about 94(A), because there the court makes it clear what is an essentially legal conclusion versus a factual finding. For example, the Trial Chamber in Karemera had found that the following facts -- the following facts were, in fact, legal conclusions or of an essentially legal nature, and the Appeals Chamber disagreed and reversed the Trial Chamber. The first one is -- it's in paragraph 26 of Karemera, the Appeals Chamber decision. It was this fact: "There were throughout Rwanda widespread or systematic attacks against a civilian population based on Tutsi ethnic identification." That contains widespread and systematic attack. Also in paragraph 26: "During the attacks, some Rwandan citizens killed or caused serious bodily or mental harm to persons perceived to be Tutsi." That contains serious bodily or mental harm. Also in paragraph 26: "Between the 1st of January, 1994, and 17 July 1994, in Rwanda, there was an armed conflict not of an international character." Paragraph 33: "Between 6 April 1994 and 17 July 1994, there was a genocide in Rwanda against the Tutsi ethnic group." Now, I would submit that all -- now, all of those -- all of those conclusions or characterisations were found by the Appeals Chamber to be factual characterisations and not essentially legal characterisations. And the Trial Chamber said that even -- that it is true that these characterisations contained phrases with legal meaning, but nonetheless they describe factual situations. They went on to say -- went on further to say that it does not matter that the facts constitute elements of the crimes charged, for example, widespread and systematic attack, armed conflict. It doesn't matter. It's still a factual conclusion; it's still a factual description. We would submit that none of the facts that are proposed by the Prosecution in this case are any different from the facts that were accepted by the Appeals Chamber in Karemera. Just to be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It would be helpful in that regard if, as against what the Appeals Chamber is saying does not constitute a legal conclusion, if an example of a legal conclusion had been given.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I can do that, Your Honour. In the Prlic case, there were a number of -- there was a motion for adjudicated facts based on prior decisions, and the -- and there's a decision dated the 7th of September, 2006. And there were a number of facts that were rejected because they were found to be essentially legal. Now, we would -- we would respectfully disagree with some of the ones that were identified by the Trial Chamber, but there are certain ones which are clearly distinct from the ones that are in Karemera or the ones that are in our case. For example, fact number 55 from the 14th of June, 2006 motion in the Prlic case -- I'm sorry, that's not fact 55 -- fact 55 in Prlic was this fact: "The detention of the BH Muslim civilians in Sovici and Doljani was unlawful and discriminatory." Fact number 63: "The Chamber finds the transfers unlawful." Now, those facts, I would submit, are distinct from the facts that we have in our case or the facts that were in Karemera, because those are extremely conclusory. To say something is unlawful does not really describe a factual situation, which is what you have when you say an attack is widespread or systematic or that there existed an armed conflict. It's -- to say something is unlawful is really purely a legal conclusion, and I think that is the distinction that -- that is where we draw the line. It's between characterisations which may use legal terms but which, nonetheless, describe a factual situation. And one test is, could you describe the same fact using other words. And so, for example, was the attack widespread and systematic? Well, yes, you could use -- you could describe that in a factual way using other words by saying the attack went on for a certain amount of time, it covered a certain amount of geographic area, it had a certain intensity. I would distinguish those facts, those types of facts, which have been found to be permissible under Karemera, and facts which are essentially legal which are really just purely a legal finding or a legal conclusion, which could not really be described factually in another way, and that is, for example, this was unlawful. So in our case, we would submit that all of the facts describe purely -- well, no, that they describe factual situations, and you could use -- you could recharacterise them using other words. It's just -- they just happen to use the words that have a legal meaning, but they nonetheless describe a factual situation. So, for example, an indirect attack. Well, you could -- that's saying -- all that's saying is that the attack was not aimed at a specific location, that it was aimed randomly, that it was not focused, not targeted. So you could find other words for it. It's saying that an indirect attack is really no different than saying an attack was widespread or systematic or that there was an armed conflict or that there was a genocide. There's no -- those are really the same type of things. They describe factual situations. And the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Genocide? Genocide against the Tutsis which the Appeals Chamber found to be factual.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes. The Appeals Chamber found that to be a factual situation, that there was a genocide against the Tutsis. Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And applying your criteria, that could be described in some other away? All the Tutsis were killed or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes. I think that -- I think that really is -- the two examples that I can think that are -- and we have to be guided by the Appeals Chamber, Your Honour, and I think that the two examples that I can think of which fall -- which are essentially legal are, number 1, saying something is just -- is that it's unlawful in a conclusory fashion like that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: May I ask, in the case of finding in relation to genocide against the Tutsis, had not the Appeals Chamber before, in another judgement, found that there was a genocide?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, the Appeals Chamber held that there was a genocide in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Right. And that's the same situation we have here, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: In a subsequent trial, to describe it as a genocide would be entirely correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Saying as to who committed it is another matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That's correct. That's exactly what Karemera said. The finding that there was a genocide could be admitted in the Karemera case -- in that case, it wasn't based on adjudicated facts; it was under 94(A) as common knowledge. But that, in part, depended on the fact that previous decisions had found it. But that is exactly the same thing we face here. An Appeals Chamber has found the facts that we proposed occurred during 1992 to 1994. It's another matter to prove that the accused had -- bears responsibility for it. So it's an identical situation, Your Honour. Now, with respect --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I was trying to find another basis for the Appeals Chamber's finding that genocide against the Tutsis was a fact, and trying to suggest that the basis might have been that the Appeals Chamber itself might have made that finding before and so it was simply following it. But I haven't read that part of the decision with sufficient care to have a conclusive opinion on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Prosecutor, you're saying that the test would be that you cannot have another word to characterise the word, or it would be difficult to say whether it is the description of a fact or the legal qualification, and you're given the example of genocide in Karemera with the Appeals Chamber judgement. But it's difficult for me to follow you. I believe - correct me if I'm wrong - that the Appeals Chamber came to that decision, which is that genocide is a common-knowledge fact, because of internal decisions made by the Trial Chamber; therefore, it is no longer necessary whenever there is a new trial for the parties to demonstrate, once again, that there has been a genocide that occurred in Rwanda. The Appeals Chamber is relying on internal decisions, but isn't there another word that we could use instead of "genocide" without qualification? I think it's very difficult. I think there is no other word, unless you qualify. Because for the moment we know that there was a genocide in Rwanda against the Tutsi; more or less 800.000 of them were killed in less than three months. But if there hadn't been the previous decision of the Trial Chamber, then you could say there was a massive slaughter of 800.000 people and only that; that might be of Tutsi ethnicities or else, period. Because we have to demonstrate genocide first and then have a legal qualification as the second step. In our case, can we qualify and consider a situation regarding the accused as we -- as can be done for genocide? I don't know. It's difficult for me to find that. If we don't rely on previous decisions of other Trial Chambers here -- I don't know if I'm very clear. The problem is the limit between the legal qualification and the name you give to a fact if there is no sound basis, robust basis, to establish a common-knowledge fact. So maybe regarding genocide, you have to explain, once again, to us how you can say that it can be considered genocide if you don't have a previous decision on that. Do you follow me?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I think, Your Honour, and I'll try my best to respond. I think, Your Honour, that in our view there are two steps. The first step is, is there a basis for recognising the fact? And under 94(A), it's common knowledge; under 94(B), it's an adjudicated fact. Now, of course, under common knowledge, the fact -- whether it's been adjudicated in a prior decision, that's also relevant. That can come into 94(A). So has it been adjudicated or is it common knowledge; yes or no? If yes, if there's a basis for it, then you proceed to the second step; and the second step is, is it a factual characterisation or is it an essentially legal characterisation? Now, with respect to genocide, I'm not familiar with -- completely, with the ins and outs of the decision with respect to genocide. But what the Appeals Chamber held is that under 94(A), there was a basis for the recognition of common -- of genocide as common knowledge because of prior decisions, because of reports, because of documents, because of the world, essentially, recognising that there was a genocide there. So you move to the second question: Is genocide a factual description or is it an essentially legal description? And Karemera answers that question. It has a -- that is directly the -- squarely the question it answers, it addresses, and we have to be guided by that. It says it is a factual description that can be judicially noticed. And in our case, to bring this to our case, we have -- step 1, we have a basis, the Galic Appeals Chamber decision which upholds the Trial Chamber's decision, which upholds these facts, so we've satisfied step 1; and then you move to step 2, which is are these factually or essentially legal? I agree that it may be sometimes difficult to draw the line between factual and essentially legal, but I would say that all of our proposed facts fall well within the line of factual, if you look at the examples provided by the Appeals Chamber in Karemera. They are no different. Saying that there was an indirect attack or that there was a civilian who was injured is no different than a widespread or systematic attack or genocide or serious bodily injury or all the things that were found to be factual in Karemera. Now, if -- the other point I would make with respect to the examples taken -- and then I'd like to move, and I think I'm going to ask for a few extra minutes, if I may, for the second issue. But the other point to make about the examples provided by the Trial Chamber in this case is that -- is to look at the testimony that has been given on these issues. And witnesses, non-experts, non-lawyers, have provided Your Honours with evidence about these issues, suggesting that they are factual issues, because, of course, witnesses cannot give you legal opinions or legal decisions. So, for example, with respect to the civilian versus military, witnesses of all types have been asked by the Prosecution, by the Defence, by the Trial Chamber, whether there were civilians present, were there military personnel. These are terms which are -- describe a factual situation and which are commonly known and commonly understood by lawyers and laypeople alike. And they are used in that way. People know what "civilian" means. It describes somebody who are not in the military, and that's how it's been used in this courtroom. The same is true with respect to indiscriminate or indirect attack. For example, Mr. -- I'm just trying to think of -- I just don't want to use a protected witness. Mr. Harland, at pages 423, 424, and 336 of the transcript talked about -- gave evidence about attacks being indiscriminate; so did Mr. Fraser at 1801, 1805 to 1806; so did Mr. Ghulam Muhammed at page 740.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, shall we, too, be given an opportunity to deal with witnesses who have been examined here? Isn't that a little out of line? We are discussing matters of principle, and now we find Mr. Whiting dealing with evidence so far given in this trial. This sounds very much like a closing argument. I think what we are dealing with here is a matter of principle, and we can't go into evidence given by witnesses before this Trial Chamber, because if we start down that path, I think I might, myself, contribute to that by listing quite a few things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Oh, yes, and you could be quite entitled to do that. I mean it's applying the principles, the law, to the factual situation. I don't see anything improper about that, and you are entitled to do that as well. But I was going to ask Mr. Whiting, in the case of an indiscriminate or indirect attack, I mean, how can you come to that conclusion without the application of a legal principle, which is derived from international humanitarian law?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Because it's purely a factual description. To say something -- it is -- it's a -- it's just an adjective which can be used outside this courtroom, outside of international law. It's used -- look at example -- at Exhibits P18 and P19. These are reports at the time made by UNPROFOR, made by non-lawyers. Remember, Mr. Harland said he's not a lawyer. He said that at page 359 of the transcript. He's not a lawyer. He's just saying that the attack was indiscriminate, meaning that it was not aimed at a certain target but was just spraying the city.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The problem I have with that is that there would hardly be anything left that would properly be described as a legal characterisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, that is a -- that is a problem which is -- that is what the law is, Your Honour, I'm afraid. The -- I agree, the category of purely legal -- essentially legal characterisations or purely legal characterisations is quite narrow, and that you'll see in looking at the Karemera decision, the Appeals Chamber decision in Karemera. It's quite narrow. If widespread or systematic is a factual characterisation, if genocide is a factual characterisation, then I agree, it is quite narrow. But that is what the law is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But in principle should it be narrow? Because it affects fundamentally the rights of the accused. These are facts of which judicial notice will be taken, meaning that you will have evidence -- meaning, rather, that the Prosecution does not have to lead evidence. It raises a rebuttable presumption which affects the burden of proof. I mean, is it proper to devise a system in such circumstances in which a category of essentially legal conclusions is so narrow? Because ultimately it will work against the interests of the accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, for -- I'd say -- make a number of responses to Your Honour. The first is that, in our view, it does not affect the burden of proof. The burden of proof remains the same and it remains on the Prosecution. It affects only the presentation of the evidence. The second is that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I mean, you're correct if by that you mean that it doesn't affect the ultimate -- the legal burden of proof. That's true. That remains under the Prosecution throughout the case. But on the particular -- on the particular piece of evidence to which it relates, if the Defence does not rebut it, the Chamber is entitled to draw a conclusion in favour of the evidence presented. That's why it is called rebuttable.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Right. But that's precisely the same as if we led the evidence, the same would be true. If we led the evidence live and the Defence did not rebut it, the same result would occur.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, not -- I don't agree. I don't agree, because a situation in which there is a rebuttable presumption in relation to a particular fact is quite distinct, in my view, from a situation in which evidence is led by the Prosecution on a particular fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I think that's a fair point, Your Honour. And I think, actually, perhaps without knowing it, we're moving slowly into the second question, because the -- the reason -- and let me just try and finish responding to Your Honour's question about is this a fair system or should it be narrow. The first response is that this has been decided. It is narrow. The Appeals Chamber has decided it, and we have to be guided by that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The Appeals Chamber didn't decide that it is narrow. That is your conclusion, or mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And if that conclusion is incorrect, then that conclusion is incorrect. But I'm just base -- that's my characterisation based on the findings that are made. And I think that if the facts that we propose are not -- are the same type as to the facts that were accepted by Karemera, then we have to be guided by that. And the second point is I do think, Your Honour, that it is a fair system, because there are two other critical protections at play here and cannot -- and we can't separate this out because there are two other critical protections. The first is that these adjudicated facts do not come easily. They are adjudicated; there's been a trial; they've been disputed; the facts have been tested; there has been cross-examination; they've been found by the Trial Chamber; they've been upheld by an Appeals Chamber. That gives the facts a certain amount of weight; they don't just come out of the air. The second point, and this is why I say that it moves into our second question, is that the facts cannot be about the accused, cannot be about the accused, and you cannot rely on these facts to convict -- solely on these facts to convict the accused, and they cannot be about the accused. So that is the second protection. So for those reasons I do think that it is appropriate for the category to be narrow, if that's the correct word to choose, or whatever the appropriate word is following from the Karemera decision. I do think that the Karemera decision is correctly decided, in other words.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, of course, we have to follow it. The question is what it means.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Correct. And I think if you -- if Your Honours look at the characterisations in that case, compare them to our case, and look at the fact that in our case the terms that have been questioned by the Trial Chamber are -- describe factual situations, civilians, military, indiscriminate attack, indirect attack, and facts about which laywitnesses, non-lawyers, have given you evidence; and if these were facts that were not facts but were of essentially legal nature, I wouldn't expect that it would be possible for witnesses to come in here and testify about it. They could not come in here and testify to Your Honours that the attack was unlawful. Your Honours would properly stop them and say, "that's for us to decide." But they have come in here and said, witness after witness has come in here and said, "they were civilians, they were military, the attacks were indirect, were indiscriminate" And that's because those describe factual situations. Now, I know Your Honours have set time limits so I'm prepared to move to the second question, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: The second question, Your Honours, in our view, it's not an issue in this case for a number of reasons. And the first reason -- the first reason is that the balance between the purposes of Rule 94(B) and the rights of the accused has already been struck by the Karemera decision, and it is this balance that is the basis for the distinction that is made in Karemera between facts which go to the acts, conduct, or mental state of the accused and all other facts. And Karemera bears a close reading to reach this conclusion. If you focus to paragraphs 47 to 52 of Karemera, paragraph 47 says that "In balancing the rights of the accused, including the right of cross-examination, versus the purposes of Rules 94(A) and 94(B)," the first point is that adjudicated facts cannot be the sole basis for conviction. That's the starting point. I mean, that's not really in dispute. The Appeal Chamber then goes on and says, Okay, so that's clearly off the table. It cannot be a sufficient basis in and of itself for a conviction. The question, then, is: Where is the line? Where is the line between facts which can be admitted and those which cannot be admitted? Paragraph 50 is important, and I'm going to quote: "Notwithstanding this point, there is nonetheless reason for caution in allowing judicial notice under Rule 94(B) of facts that are central to the criminal responsibility of the accused, for ordinarily in criminal cases the burden of production and persuasion are on the Prosecution. Although the latter always remains on the Prosecution, even shifting the former has significant implications for the accused's procedural rights, in particular, his right to hear and confront the witnesses against him." To pause for a moment, the Appeals Chamber is saying the issue here is about the accused's procedural rights and his rights to confront the evidence. They go on: "The Appeals Chamber considers that as a result," in other words, as a result of this concern about balancing the purposes of the rule versus the procedural rights of the accused, "as a result, an exclusion for judicial notice under Rule 94(B) is appropriate but one narrower than that adopted by the Trial Chamber. Judicial notice should not be taken of adjudicated facts relating to the acts, conduct, and mental state of the accused." So -- and then in paragraph 51, the Appeals Chamber goes on and makes the point again, it says: "This interpretation," in other words, this rule that the facts cannot go to the acts, conduct, or mental state of the accused, "strikes a balance between the procedural rights of the accused and the interest of expediency that is consistent with the one expressly struck in Rule 92 bis." So the Court has struck the balance, Your Honours, between the procedural rights of the accused, including the right to confrontation and to test the evidence, and the purposes of Rule 94(A) and Rule 94(B), in particular 94(B). And where the balance is struck is excluding evidence which goes to the acts, conduct, and mental state of the accused. Just as an aside, in order to get clarity on what that means, the Trial Chamber -- I'm sorry, the Appeals Chamber cites, then, to paragraphs 10 and 11 of the Galic appeal decision on an interlocutory appeal, dated 7 June 2002. And those paragraphs 10 and 11 of Galic are also instructive. They refer to 92 bis, but the Appeals Chamber is saying that the situations are the same, 92 bis and 94(B). The test is the same. And in paragraphs 10 and 11 of the Galic appeals interlocutory decision, the Appeals Chamber makes it clear what it means when it says "facts that go to the acts, conduct, and mental state of the accused." It makes that point very clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: In our case, one may say that a number of acts do not go to the acts and conduct of the accused, but what is meant by "mental state" if the facts are to be relied upon to prove that the accused knew, should have known, or was put on notice that crimes had been, or were about to be, committed? Is that not something going to his mental state?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: No. No, Your Honour, it is not. And the Karemera decision, in particular the reference to paragraphs 10 and 11 of the Galic decision, make that absolutely clear. They say that this -- that it is permissible to admit facts of -- for example, facts of subordinates, and then argue that because of the position of the accused, he must have known of what was happening. That is permissible. That is explicitly set out. Paragraph 11 of the Appeals Chamber decision in Galic says: "The conduct of an accused person necessarily includes his relevant state of mind, so that a written statement which goes to proof of any act or conduct of the accused upon which the Prosecution relies to establish that state of mind is not admissible under Rule 92 bis," and of course would not be admissible under Rule 94(B) either. "In order to establish that state of mind, however, the Prosecution may rely upon the acts and conduct of others which have been proved by Rule 92 bis statements." The same would apply with 94(B). "An easy example would be proof in relation to Article 5 of the Tribunal's Statute of the knowledge by the accused, that his acts fit into a pattern of wide-spread or systematic attacks directed against a civilian population." And here's the kicker: "Such knowledge may be inferred from evidence of such a pattern of attacks proved by Rule 92 bis statements, "or Rule 94 B, "that he must have known that his own acts," proved by oral evidence, "fitted into that pattern." The second point, Your Honours, on this issue -- in other words, the first point is that we believe that Karemera has already struck this balance that has been -- this issue that has been identified by the Trial Chamber between the rights of the accused, including the right to cross-examine, and the purposes of Rule 94(B) and that is the basis for the distinction, and none of the facts that we propose go to the acts, conduct, or mental state of the accused. None of them. The second point, Your Honours, is that in this case there is no danger to the rights of the accused, including the right to cross-examine, because -- and this is why I started the argument the way I did, because the Defence has taken the position that the proposed facts are irrelevant, that they are irrelevant. In other words, in some -- the Defence has really taken the opposite position of the position that has been inquired about by the Trial Chamber, which has -- the question suggests that the issues are so important that the Defence must have the opportunity to cross-examine and test the evidence. But the Defence has taken the position that it's irrelevant; forget about it. So there is no need to -- there is no danger, because they're not interested in those issues. They're not important for their case, for their defence. So there's no danger. There's no need for them, in particular, to test these facts. The third point, Your Honours, is that the facts that we propose to admit into evidence, while relevant, while important, for the reasons that I have set forth, are nonetheless one step removed from the crime base of this case. And to make the point, I've actually made a chart which I'd like to offer to Your Honours and maybe it could be placed on the ELMO. It's a simple chart to make what I think is a simple point. Your Honours, under the Appeals Chamber decision in Karemera [French on English channel]. We're getting French on the English channel. Under the decision in Karemera, and I've quoted there from paragraph 52, which is kind of the conclusion of the discussion from paragraphs 47 to 52, the facts which go to the accused box number 1 can clearly not be admitted under Rule 94(B), which is why it's red. Facts, however, in box 2, the crime base, can be admitted under Rule 94(B). That is the decision in Karemera. What we are proposing is one step removed, and this is important for the rights of the accused, and it's the facts in box number 3. And I've already set forth why those facts are relevant to our case. They are alleged in the indictment. They are important for the establishment of the crime, but they are nonetheless one step removed. And, for example, if we -- if the facts were admitted and we proved the position of the accused, we could not argue a conviction on that basis alone. We would still have to prove the facts in box number 2. Whereas if we admitted box number 2 under 94(B) and then proved by oral evidence the facts in box number 1, that could be a sufficient basis for a conviction. Now, our argument is that if the facts in box number 2 can be admitted by Rule 94(B), then it necessarily follows - it necessarily follows - that the facts in box number 3 can be admitted under Rule 94(B), consistent with the rights of the accused. And the contrary is also true, that if there were a finding that the facts in number 3 could not be admitted because the accused had the right to cross-examine or had the right to test them, then I cannot imagine a situation - I cannot imagine a situation - where you could get facts in box number 2 admitted, because they are closer, they are more essential, more important, to the accused. So, in other words, to give Karemera any meaning, to give Rule 94(B) any force - and that is the whole point of Karemera is that it's giving -- it says specifically 94(B) should not be rendered a dead letter - to give 94(B) any meaning, the facts in box number 3 have to be admissible. And I would ask, Your Honours, if this could be made either an exhibit or made a filing, just so it's part of the record, this chart; otherwise, it's going to be hard to follow on the record later what I'm talking about with respect to box 1, 2, and 3. Two final points to make on this issue, Your Honours. One I've already made but I'll reiterate is that the facts from the Galic decision, the facts that we seek to admit, have been tested in a trial by Judges, by a Defence. They've been cross-examined; they've been found by the Trial Chamber; they've been found by the Appeals Chamber. Now, when the facts are about the accused, it's not sufficient that they've been tested, because the Appeals Chamber in Karemera said that there could be -- that the prior accused might have interests to blame a subsequent accused. It's not good enough. In other words, this accused in our case should have the right to test facts that are about him, but that right does not necessarily -- does not necessarily have that that right with respect to facts which are not about him and which have been tested already. And in this case, they've been tested by an accused who had all the same interests, all the same perspective that this accused had.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But they are being used to establish his responsibility under 7.3.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Not under 7.3, more under 7.1. Perhaps under 7.3, you're right, Your Honour. That's true --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So I don't know how it can be said not to affect the accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, I was not clear. What I meant is that they are -- I was trying to rely on the Karemera distinction. They are not facts which are about the acts, conduct, or mental state of the accused. It is true that they affect the accused; otherwise, they would not be relevant. And then the last point, Your Honours, is the point which you yourself have identified which is that these facts -- an additional protection is that these facts can be rebutted. In conclusion, with respect to both of your questions, Your Honours, it's our view that the Karemera Appeals Chamber decision provides guidance on those issues and that following the Karemera Appeals Chamber decision, the facts that we have proposed should be admitted for the purposes that we have proposed them, and that to not admit those facts would be, in our view, to render 94(B), really, a dead letter. And the only thing that could then come in under Rule 94(B) is background facts, like the date that Bosnia-Herzegovina was recognised, things like that, which are more usually the subject of agreed facts and which are not really the purpose of Rule 94(B). In order to give purpose and to give force to Rule 94(B), which is what the Karemera Appeals Decision says we must do, these facts should be admitted, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Can I just try to apply, in practice, some of your arguments, because I'm not quite convinced of what is the correct interpretation of the law as it is -- as it appears at this moment. I mean, what I'm saying is that I believe that there is probably still room for some developments in the law and in the case law practice of this Tribunal. Let's have a look, just for instance, at the last of your proposed adjudicated facts, fact number 181, and tell me, Mr. Prosecutor, how this is not a legal finding and does not infringe in any way on the rights of the accused and the protection of justice. The fact reads, and I quote, "The military attacks on civilians in ABiH-held areas of Sarajevo, between September 1992 and August 1994, carried out with a specific purpose to spread terror among that civilian population constituted a campaign of sniping and shelling against civilians." Now, it would seem to me that if you are asking the Chamber to accept this fact and establish that this may come into evidence with the force of judicial notice, then you're asking us to accept that the sniping and shelling that took place between 1992 and 1994 was carried out with the specific purpose, to spread terror, and thus constituted a crime, I guess, against the civilian population, and that it also constituted a campaign. Now, this would seem to be asking us to accept without further proof the allegations that you are holding against the accused; namely, that there was a campaign of shelling and sniping and, indirectly, a campaign of terror. Now, this is what you're asking us to accept with a force of judicial notice, and I just don't know if that would be correct. It would seem to me to imply that the accused, if this fact were to be admitted as judicial notice, that the accused would be faced with a very burdensome fact for which he had not himself seen the proof in the evidence and on which he had not had the chance to cross-examine.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you for your question, Your Honour. I disagree, however, for a number of reasons. The first reason is that the -- I would submit that -- and, again, the line is not easy to draw, but I would submit that the -- what is set out here is a factual -- ultimately is a factual description. That's the first point. That the attacks were -- had a purpose and that there was a campaign. That describes a factual situation. The second point is that we could not hold these facts --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Excuse me, counsel, because to say that an action had a specific purpose is not just a factual observation; it would seem to me it would require the intent of the perpetrator, an assessment of why was this done, and under which conditions. It's more than just a fact. You're looking into the mind of a person and you're telling us, Oh, yes, he or she had the purpose to do this or do that. That's a very far-reaching fact, I'd say.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, again, we have to be guided by Karemera, but that is a factual inquiry. What Your Honour just described is a factual inquiry, looking into the mind of the perpetrator. Now, of course, it has legal consequences and there are legal terms that are used, but it is ultimately a factual inquiry. What was the purpose of the perpetrator? Why did he do it? And you'll have witnesses that come in and say, well, he did it for this reason, he did it for that reason, or no, I didn't do it for that reason. The witnesses testify about the purposes of the attack. They testify about the fact that there was a campaign. And they can testify about it because they are factual inquiries.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I don't think witnesses normally testify about the purpose, because we -- I mean, they testify about the attack, and submissions are then made by the parties as to the inference to be drawn as to the purpose. But if a witness were to testify that the purpose of the attack was to do so and so, counsel on the other side might object and the objection might very well be upheld.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have to disagree with that. Your Honour, you are absolutely correct that most of the time purpose or intent is inferred, and that -- but that is only because of the nature of the evidence we have before us. Oftentimes, we do not have direct evidence about intent or purpose because we don't have somebody who spoke to the perpetrator. But if we had -- if we had somebody who was standing next to the perpetrator at the time of an attack and who came in here and testified that the perpetrator said, "I am committing this attack because of this reason," that evidence would certainly be admissible and would be relevant and would be factual. It's just that we usually don't have that kind of evidence. We've gotten used to inferring intent from the consequences, from the ongoing pattern. But if we had evidence of direct intent, and when we do, for example, through statements of the accused or -- not the accused, the perpetrator or a diary of the perpetrator, then that evidence would certainly be admissible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Suppose the perpetrator will say, "Well, yes, I did this but it wasn't for the purpose of spreading terror. No, it was for the purpose of responding to attacks."

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That evidence would certainly be admissible, and we often get that kind of evidence. In other words, the Prosecution often brings evidence, saying -- Your Honour, you're shaking your head --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Because you're arguing beyond the point. My point is that if there are alternative interpretations of why the perpetrator did what he did, then it would seem to me to be difficult to accept that it is only the one interpretation that should apply and not the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, that's a rule about inferences and -- and there are rules about when you can draw inferences. And if there's more than one inference available and one points to guilt and one points to not guilt, then generally the rule is that you cannot draw the inference of guilt. That's correct. But the question here is -- the question here is whether this evidence is factual or legal, and my point is that evidence with respect to purpose or intent, whether it's direct evidence or circumstantial evidence, is factual and admissible, and we have witnesses who testify about it. It may have a legal consequence, but those are factual issues. What is in the mind of the perpetrator? That's a factual inquiry. Now, the second point, Your Honour, is that we -- is that these facts are not about the time period of the accused. They're 1992 to 1994. So we could not prove these facts and draw any conclusions about the guilt of the accused, because they're not the right time period. And that's the point of the chart. These facts are not from this box; they're from this box. They're one step removed, which is further protection for the accused. The third point, Your Honour, the third point is that we could not draw any conclusions without presenting linkage evidence by evidence that can be tested, by oral evidence or whatever evidence -- however we admit it, of the accused. And that's the whole point of Karemera is that the crime base can be -- that can be judicially noticed under 94(B). It's the linkage evidence connecting it to the accused that still has to be proven in the trial. And the final point, Your Honour, is, again, the accused himself has taken the position that these facts from 1992 to 1994 are irrelevant, so I can't see where, then, the danger is to the accused. But the most -- but the most important point is that number --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I wouldn't attach too much importance to that. That's a sort of procedural point. It is still for the Trial Chamber to determine whether there is a proper basis for judicial notice.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I agree with that, but again I think that has to go done, to some extent, in the context -- not in a vacuum, but in the context of the defence that has been chosen by this Defence, by this accused. And I think that is a right of the accused, to choose his defence, and there should be deference granted to that. But the most important point, Your Honours, is that under Karemera that these sorts that are not -- that are about the crimes, that are about the crimes, can be admitted by judicial notice. And here more so than in Karemera, because, as I said, they're about a different time period. About his time period, box number 2, no judicial notice; we're proving it all in the trial. It's box number 3 that we're seeking to admit. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I thank you. Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, as a lawyer, and I have been one for 40 years now, I have never found myself in a situation more difficult than this one. Having heard what Mr. Whiting has said, I am not quite sure that I can respond fully. I will try to spend half as much time as Mr. Whiting did and to raise several matters. If Mr. Whiting wishes to propose this as evidence, please note this: Mr. Whiting is oversimplifying matters. He is trying to illustrate certain matters with a chart such as this one. My assistant has drawn my attention to it because I do not speak English. First, he has to prove this arrow connecting the two green squares and only then can he tender this into evidence. My learned friend, Mr. Whiting, has tendered this a moment ago, if my understanding is correct. I may be mistaken, but it seems to me that he tendered this into evidence as an exhibit. That's point number 1. Secondly, as counsel, together with my entire team, I find myself in a very difficult situation where I have to deal with these topical matters without, at the same time, compromising the case that I wish to present before you on behalf of the accused. It will be very difficult for me to address these matters. I hope that over the break I will have time enough to put my submissions together. But let me tell this at once, and with full certainty: In the period whilst he was in command of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, General Dragomir Milosevic and me, as his counsel, will not bring before this Tribunal a single witness who already testified in other cases in the past years. What I will do is try and have certain documents dating from that period through some of our witnesses into evidence. I will do that. However, I will not be using a single witness who testified back then, and I will not resort to any rules allowing me to do this. And I'm speaking of international and national witnesses alike. Another matter. I have to say, and this is no flattery, I do trust this Trial Chamber greatly, and I do trust that they will deal with these matters properly. The accused who stands here before you will never try to shift any blame onto anyone else. Toward the end of the day today, I will propose to show you a map that will best illustrate to you the truthfulness of some matters that I will say. Mr. Whiting touched upon these matters, but I assure you that the accused will not shift any blame, if any, of course, onto anyone else. And I could not believe my ears when Mr. Whiting theatrically gestured, motioning to the head, and he meant the head of the accused. And I'm telling you that the criminal responsibility has its individual side, which means that unless what was in his head at the time of these events is proven, then the whole charge will not stand. We have to look at the -- what we could do is look at the adjudicated facts from Galic and then just agree on matters and leave the courtroom. This is something that Mr. Whiting seems to have suggested today. I, on my part, after working with my team, am prepared to present you our positions with regard to the issues raised by the Trial Chamber this morning. As the break is nearing, I will only touch upon several other matters. Mr. Whiting said something else that I could hardly believe. I suppose that the interpreters will have difficulty in interpreting what I have to say. He said, if I understand correctly, that sometimes it is important to reduce the judicial system or to narrow it down. I may be mistaken; maybe I misunderstood. But he said that sometimes it is necessary to narrow down the judicial system. This can never be done in the context of someone's criminal responsibility being determined. To draw parallels between this particular case and some other cases that were qualified differently cannot be done. Mr. Whiting spent a great deal of time talking about matters that are incomparable, absolutely incomparable, in the legal sense. The matters that we'll be dealing with and the Trial Chamber will be dealing with in this case cannot be compared with the matters that Mr. Whiting talked about. I will be quite brief in my submissions after the break, when I look at my notes concerning what Mr. Whiting said. Mr. Whiting said that the Defence challenged only two facts, or, rather, only one fact, which is "carried out a long-term campaign of shelling and sniping." Let me just find this in my notes. Facts from paragraph -- let me just find the number. Facts 54 and 55. If I'm mistaken, it doesn't really matter --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: He said that the Defence challenged one set of facts, those from proposed facts from 54 to 181. Not one fact but one set comprising those from 54 to 181.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, let me just emphasise this: We spoke about facts 54 and 55 where we said that this was a qualification. In challenging this characterisation, we actually challenged all the facts. That is the gist of our position that I orally presented at the time, and we weren't discussing these matters at all. In the indictment, in item 1, that's the most important part of the indictment --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Those facts which were challenged as being definitions, did you?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I meant to. Those two, 54 and 55, we would not pursue. I think they could be called legal clarifications or definitions, and I'm happy to drop those.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thanks. I think that's a concession well made. He's not pursuing those facts, 54 to 55. I believe we'll take the break now. We'll take the break now for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the break has been very helpful to me. My idea is to give up my probably meaningless polemic with the esteemed Prosecutor, Mr. Whiting, and that is precisely why I'll be moving straight to the questions that you raised while addressing both parties, the questions that deserve answers. What our team has done is to define a number of positions, and I will read this slowly. This could be summarised in the form of several decisive conditions. I really believe that the formal conditions for the application of Rule 94(B) have been met. We do, however, also believe that those facts are not relevant and are in no way helpful to these proceedings. We also believe that the price of their application might be to prejudice the rights of the accused. In addition to that, if the Trial Chamber believes that the conditions for Rule 94(B) have been met, especially as concerns the relevance of facts to the case in hand, we believe that such terms as "civilians" and "indiscriminate attacks" or "legitimacy of targets" constitute legal matters and not factual matters. The objective of 94(B), Rule 94(B), is to expedite proceedings as a whole, to speed up the trial, if you like. Nevertheless, this only applies under the condition that the right of the accused to a fair defence is not prejudiced, and the same goes for the right of the Defence team to properly cross-examine witnesses. It is the position of this Defence that these facts are inaccurate, even if they have been confirmed in the Galic case, and therefore cannot be used in the present trial of General Dragomir Milosevic. In their motion dated the 25th of January, the OTP are themselves in contradiction, in practical terms. In their motion dated the 18th of December, 2006, they quote the relevant jurisprudence accurately, the jurisprudence to do with the application of Rule 94(B). They provide the criteria for the application of that particular rule, and, among other things, they state as follows: "These facts do not directly or incorrectly prove the criminal responsibility of the accused, his behaviour, or his acts, or his mens rea." In their motion dated the 25th of January, they say that although General Milosevic does not stand indicted in relation to the period before he became the commander of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps in August 1994, it still cannot be said that he was not aware of the shelling and sniping campaign against the civilian population that was in progress throughout that period, especially in view of the positions in which he was incumbent within the SRK in August -- prior to August 1994. Just one fact for the benefit of the Chamber. Two days before he took up his position, or, rather, four days, on the 14th of August, 1994, regardless of everything that is addressed here as a possibility, he immediately signed an Anti-Sniping Agreement thereby, at least in his own head, displaying a different attitude towards the issues at that time, because this same agreement had not been signed for a long time simply because nobody was able to get it signed. There were several months of truce with regard to sniping following this agreement, which clearly shows his mens rea and his personal attitude towards the problems that were happening at the time. If I may be excused this slight digression, I would like to wrap up in the following way: The only conclusion that we can possibly reach is that the OTP have here proposed a twisted application, a totally twisted application of the relevant jurisprudence, which, among other things, they managed to misquote in one of their motions. The OTP have been addressing certain issues with regard to the evidence so far in this trial. May I be allowed to say a couple of things based on what we have heard from witnesses so far. I will only take five or six minutes more to complete my submissions. I'm sure the Trial Chamber remembers we had the witness Mr. Nicolai, who was the number two man of NATO at his time on duty. The pages are 1057, lines 10 through 12. My question was: [as read] "Yesterday, you spoke about the proportion or the fact that at least three shells had to be fired in order to neutralise a target, such as a moving vehicle that is firing. What would a proportionate reaction would be? Would it be to fire several shells when someone is firing randomly? It is necessary for the other party to be effective to use a large number of shells in order to crush the enemy's operation. Can that be considered an appropriate answer?" And then General Nicolai goes on to say: "In my opinion, the criterion here is not the number of shells. The criterion is the position being targeted. As long as the firing is against the position from which the shells were fired, that would be a justified response." 1058, lines 1 through 2: "But you said yesterday that it took several shells to make sure the target was hit. You can't just fire one shell and still be sure a target was hit, unless, of course, you fire randomly. Did I understand your reply, sir? Yes; am I right?" And the reply, "Yes. You understood me correctly? The proportion is always there when a significant number of shells were fired against a position that the original firing had come from." That's the first thing. And something else, too. General Nicolai, who is a well-regarded NATO officers, said before this Chamber that every young man, every boy in Sarajevo was, in fact, carrying a weapon at the time. And now I'm asking myself and you, Your Honours, has a single sniping incident been proved beyond a reasonable doubt so far? You heard from General Fraser who said that a sniper always hits when aiming. For the most part, what we had here was BH army officers firing at their own people, fragmentation bullets being used, where a single fragmentation bullet injures several persons. Another thing we often encountered were stray bullets. That wraps up my submissions, Your Honour, and I have nothing to add, unless the Chamber has questions for me. After that, I would like to make an application. Just to make the Court's work, I will be tendering this later through a witness. It is important for me to show that document now so that in closed session I might be able to tell you what I'm supposed to do tomorrow. If I had to explain that, I wouldn't have to explain the motion regarding your decision, some things. I wish to show a map --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What is it -- you're seeking to tender something now in relation to your submissions?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, in a way, it's to do with the arguments discussed today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And especially to do with the things that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The practice that I'm accustomed to from my experience is not to admit documents such as the one submitted by the Prosecution as an exhibit but to treat it as an aide-memoire, and that is what I propose to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Your Honours, what I'm trying to show you now -- the reason I'm showing you this is so you can help the Defence to maybe half our cross-examinations, the totality of our cross-examinations. On the other hand, I would like to explain something in closed session which is equally important. This is the copy, the original, of a document which I received from the archive of the army of the army of Republika Srpska. I'm sure that the Prosecutor has the same map but they have not been using it so far. This is a decision by Dragomir Milosevic which was approved by General Ratko Mladic, and this decision clearly shows what I'm trying to point out here, a decision taken by ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, I suggest that the tendering map be left until later when we are dealing with the adducing of evidence and I will consider that later, but right now I want to close off the argument on judicial notice.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, that precisely is the reason I'm doing this, to make your ruling more proper. I don't wish to tire you. I can't explain this. What you asked me to do by tomorrow, I'd like to do that in closed session. It's a map. It's a map that I might as well be tendering in two or three days. I really don't know. I'll have to be tendering it, but I think it might be very helpful for you to have a look.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, let me conclude the hearing on judicial notice. Judge Harhoff has a question for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Just before we close, and I believe we should close now, I would be grateful if counsel could explain to the Chamber just how you would respond to the two questions that the Chamber put to you; namely, where and how do you distinguish between factual findings and findings of an essential legal nature, and how do you deal with the relation between the purposes of Rule 94 and the interests of justice? Could you kindly and briefly explain to us the positions that the Defence has taken?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Judge Harhoff, you mentioned a while ago paragraph 181, and you asked the Prosecutor about that. My position on all these paragraphs is the same. My position on all the issues mentioned here, 1 through 181, the paragraph that you mentioned a while ago, my position, as lead counsel for the Defence, as well as my colleague, is just that: None of these facts can possibly have any bearing on what occurred during General Dragomir Milosevic's time as commander. In my understanding, this is a different case altogether, in every way, especially in terms of the time frame. There are issues that I can't address at the present time, issues that I might be indicating throughout our defence case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: So you would agree in the Prosecution's characterisation of your submission as being, simply, "the facts are irrelevant"?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is my belief that they are irrelevant and that they should, in no way, trouble this Chamber. I don't think the Chamber should be placing such things into the e-court system. It is entirely irrelevant, especially in relation to what I have just shared with you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Tapuskovic, one little point. I followed very closely what you said in answer to the Prosecutor's submission, but do you believe that this Trial Chamber must use Rule 94(B) or not, notably regarding the historical background. There are facts. You know, when I read the Prosecutor's motion, for example, the Prosecutor will be mentioning 1945; 1990; the SFRY which was made up of six republics. I think this, you have already accepted this. So can this Trial Chamber use this at least? And then furthermore, later, later on, for item 44 in the Prosecutor's motion, [In English] "After the JNA partially withdrew the parliament of Republika Srpska on 12 May 1992, ordered the formation of the Bosnian Serb army, VRS." [Interpretation] So do you accept all this, or not. If so, you cannot reject the Trial Chamber using Rule for a number of facts, because there I don't follow you. I don't follow you in your oral submission. Is it the whole process that is not relevant, or are you picking and choosing some facts on an ad hoc basis?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's difficult at this time to answer in a straightforward manner, but I'll do my best. The historical circumstances and the general situation are not really things that I'll be looking into to any great degree, in my case. We need that perspective, needless to say; however, not done this way, not done as presented in these facts. My approach to these issues will be strictly limited, and I can't accept them like this, as something that is generally relevant. I'll be trying to show, especially in the early days of the clashes, some of the facts have been erroneously ascertained. That's my understanding. I might as well be wrong. These are issues to do with history. I will be dealing with those, too, but to a very limited extent, because the problem of what was happening in Sarajevo and around Sarajevo at the time has precious little to do with the historical context. If there is a general context to be dealt with, I will have to deal with it, but certainly not in the way that was formulated in the final judgement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, Mr. Tapuskovic. We'll, therefore, treat as an aide-memoire the document submitted by the Prosecution. And do you have one to submit as an aide-memoire?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is the map, Your Honours, because of your previous order to explain some things by tomorrow about what you had previously ordered us. The map can be very useful for that purpose. I'll be tendering that as an exhibit in one or two days, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: In one or two days, yes. Well, I'd just like to thank both parties for their submissions, and the Chamber will take them into account in arriving at its decision on this matter. May I now ask Mr. Whiting, or the Prosecutor, to call his next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry to have to address you again, Your Honours. I will not be able to provide a reply by tomorrow unless you have seen this document, which has to do with the order that you gave me. Can I do this in closed session, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, closed session. Private session. Do we need closed session or just private?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in private session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President and Your Honours. May I proceed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-54 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: I trust that you are feeling better now?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-54 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not in the best of health.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-54 [Resumed]
utterances.text: But it's better than it was before.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Well, I don't plan to be very long with you today, and if you could keep your answers brief, that would be of much help. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness -- Ms. Isailovic, do you -- Witness, that concludes your evidence. Thank you for giving it, and you may now leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thank you very, very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's just been brought to my attention that none of the statements of this witness have been admitted.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, in fact, I found that out, so I have a list of documents for you. First, for Fraser, for Witness Fraser, would you like me to do it now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So the statement of Mr. Fraser, DD00-0522.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D52, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then, Your Honour, I showed to Mr. Fraser order coming from Vahid Karavelic, DD00-0573.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, it's admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D53, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And we have the statement of the witness of today, DD00-0471.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Sorry, does counsel have a date for that statement?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 15 November 1995.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be admitted as Exhibit D54.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then we have the statement of the 20th of May, 2006, DD00-0479.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D55, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And, lastly, the official report of the investigation of the 22nd of November, 1994, DD00-0489.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, if these statements refer to the previous witness, then they should be admitted under seal, since he was protected, firstly. And, secondly, I would just like to mention one thing. As Mr. President and Your Honours will recall, before this witness gave his evidence, Mr. Whiting explained that there had been a discrepancy and that we had clarified certain matters in proofing, and there has been a note to that effect disclosed to the Defence on the 5th of February, 2007. Therefore, if learned counsel intends to have these statements admitted, I would ask that this information report similarly be admitted into evidence, under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let's deal with the first thing. You're saying that all of these statements, you would wish to have them admitted under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. They are to be admitted under seal. Is that clear to the court deputy?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The two exhibits that we -- the one statement that we have admitted so far and assigned an exhibit number would be D54, and that would be under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Lest there be any confusion, I mean with reference to Witness 54, not to Mr. Fraser.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. I think that was understood. Witness 54. Now, the other matter you raised was -- what is this, a statement of clarification?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Correct, Mr. President. In proofing the witness, it became clear that the witness was injured by -- as he, indeed, has given evidence today and last time he was in court, by a shell and not a bullet. And you may recall that Mr. Whiting made submissions just prior to the commencement of this witness' evidence. Therefore, if learned counsel is seeking to admit these statements where, indeed, it is stated that he was injured by a bullet, then I would ask that the information report be similarly admitted into evidence, under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Has that been shown to the Chamber or to the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: The Defence certainly has it. And, in fact, I didn't show it to the witness in examination-in-chief because he has spoken about it under oath here. However, when learned counsel was putting certain questions to the witness, for the sake of completeness and clarity with respect to the shelling incident and the sniping incident and the discrepancy of these incidents, that information report --
